front: What are the three top-level requirements an algorithm must satisfy? (Bestimmt, Berechenbar, Anwendbar)
back: Determined (same input → same output & same steps), Computable (finite, terminates, executable), Applicable (general and correct).

front: Determiniertheit vs. Determinismus — what's the difference?
back: Determiniertheit: same input always gives the same output. Determinismus: same input always produces the exact same sequence of steps/intermediate states.

front: What are the three parts of a standard correctness proof for a sorting algorithm?
back: 1) Termination, 2) Sortedness (via loop invariant), 3) Permutation property (no elements lost or invented).

front: Schleifeninvariante (loop invariant) — what is it used for?
back: A condition true before, during, and after every loop iteration; used to prove an algorithm's correctness by induction.

front: Finit vs. Terminierbar — what's the difference?
back: Finit: the algorithm's description itself has finite length (theoretical). Terminierbar: the algorithm actually halts in finite time on any input (practical).

front: Name three reasons you might deliberately choose a LESS efficient algorithm.
back: Easier to formally verify; avoiding a runtime side-channel (constant-time algorithms leak less), so worst-case-always behavior beats fast-on-average; a highly parallel algorithm may do more total work but finish faster in wall-clock time.

front: Besides raw time, name three other resources an algorithm might be optimized for.
back: Variance of runtime (constant-time algorithms), size of the algorithm itself (chip area / lines of code), and parallelizability.

front: In a loop invariant for 'find the largest index where a run-condition holds', why is a separate conditionTrue flag needed instead of just tracking the latest valid index?
back: Because a single violation must LATCH false for every later iteration -- once the run-condition fails once, no later index can be valid even if it locally satisfies the condition again.
